item.title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite (206 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://zerodha.tech/blog/high-performance-distributed-blob-storage/, See on Hacker News

TLDR; We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.

On Kite, our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.

Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB (ssdb), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.

Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:

  1. SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable.
  2. Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads.

As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:

  • A key-value blob store with a simple API.
  • Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets.
  • Horizontally scalable, distributed.
  • Disk-space efficiency / compression.
  • Easily maintainable and highly economical.

So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:

  • ScyllaDB: We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB.
  • PostgreSQL: We already have considerable experience with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as BYTEA columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency.
  • YugabyteDB: Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features.
  • RocksDB: Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes.
  • Ceph: Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out.
  • SeaweedFS: This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts.
  • S3 and MinIO: Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Not to mention, S3 would incur significant costs given thousands of ops per second and tens of millions of ops per day.
  • Raw filesystem (one file per blob): Putting blobs directly on disk meant implementing atomic writes and write batching, managing large numbers of files and directories, good old atomic read/write disk performance and inode headaches, and maintaining a separate metadata index for TTLs. Not to mention, orchestrating this over AWS storage volumes.

Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its 35% Faster Than The Filesystem claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates millions of tables every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?

So we ended up building Blobasaur, an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.

What we needed

We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:

  • Redis protocol compatibility (if possible at all): Every existing client already used standard Redis libraries (GET, SET, HGET, HSET, DEL, EXPIRE). If we could get a system that could be a drop-in replacement, that would allow us to leave existing services untouched and reduce risk significantly.
  • Low latency across payload sizes: It needed to serve both 2 KB settings blobs and 5 MB chart layouts with single-digit millisecond latency.
  • Built-in compression: Almost all our payloads are repetitive JSON, which compresses well.
  • Simple CRUD with TTLs: We didn’t need complex data structures, server-side scripting, or secondary queries. We just needed key-value and hash CRUD with key expiry.
  • Multi-node partitioning: We needed to split data across multiple machines so a single node wasn’t a bottleneck.
  • Relaxed durability is acceptable: This store holds non-critical UI and workspace preferences, and not critical financial data. If a sudden power loss drops recent writes, a user might lose a recent chart layout tweak, which is annoying, but it never affects trading. This was a good performance trade-off for our use case.

Why SQLite (and Rust)

We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:

  • Atomic writes and batching.
  • TTL cleanup, which needs secondary indexes or walking the directories.
  • Dealing with fd limits.
  • Managing metadata separately from the raw data.

SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.

Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard sqlite3 CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.

While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust (sqlx, rusqlite, and tokio), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.

Architecture

Splitting data into shards

In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.

To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards:

  • Consistent hashing: Each key maps to one shard via multi-probe consistent hashing.
  • Per-shard writer with group commit: Each shard has a dedicated writer task fed by a bounded queue. Instead of committing one key at a time, the writer drains a batch of pending writes from the queue and executes them inside a single BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT transaction. This amortizes transaction and WAL overhead across concurrent clients.
  • Concurrent readers: Reads go directly to a per-shard pool of read-only SQLite connections and can run concurrently with the writer.

How much does sharding help?

We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x.

All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and batch_size = 50, with the data directory on tmpfs to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections.

Workload1 shard16 shards
HSET only7,740 ops/s, p99 10.7 ms25,324 ops/s, p99 8.3 ms
50% HSET, 50% HGET14,227 ops/s, p99 10.5 ms29,538 ops/s, p99 8.5 ms
HGET only67,128 ops/s, p99 2.1 ms70,884 ops/s, p99 2.3 ms

With 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention.

At 25,324 HSET operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly 1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources.

Schema

Our services use both plain keys (SET/GET) and Redis hashes (HSET/HGET) to group blobs by service or feature (for example, HSET prefs userID <json>).

Inside each shard, plain keys live in a blobs table:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blobs (
    key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    data BLOB,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    expires_at INTEGER,
    version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_expires_at
    ON blobs(expires_at)
    WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL;

SET writes to blobs. HSET writes to a table for its namespace, blobs_<namespace>, with the same columns. For example, HSET prefs user42 ... stores user42 in blobs_prefs.

Expiry is stored in expires_at on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ?), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on expires_at is a partial index (WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index.

Compression

Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production.

Here is the compression ratio across one hour of production HSET traffic:

HSET payloadSent by the clientStored in SQLiteReduction
Average63.6 KiB5.5 KiBabout 11x
p99935 KiB59.3 KiBabout 16x

With SQLite’s default 4 KiB pages, shrinking a 63.6 KiB payload to 5.5 KiB reduces its storage footprint from roughly 16 pages to roughly 2, before accounting for row and index overhead. Fewer pages holding blob data means less pressure on the page cache and less data to write through the WAL and into the database.

Durability

Because we don’t require strict durability for our specific use case of UI preferences, shards run in WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL. SQLite does not fsync on every transaction commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent committed transactions that have not yet been synced to durable storage, while preserving database consistency.

For workloads that want even lower write latency, Blobasaur also supports an optional async_write mode that acknowledges writes as soon as they enter the shard’s memory queue, before the SQLite batch commits.

Scaling across machines

To scale beyond a single server, Blobasaur implements the Redis Cluster protocol, making it compatible with standard cluster-aware Redis clients. Like Redis Cluster, the keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots using CRC16. Each Blobasaur node owns a configured range of slots, and nodes discover each other via gossip. If a client sends a key to the wrong node, the node responds with a MOVED redirect pointing to the owner node.

This gives Blobasaur two-level routing:

  1. Cluster level: CRC16(key) % 16384 selects the machine.
  2. Node level: Multi-probe consistent hashing selects the SQLite shard on that machine.

There are some limitations right now. At present, slot assignment is static in config. Live slot rebalancing between running nodes and automatic failover are not implemented yet.

Changing the number of shards

We chose multi-probe consistent hashing so resharding a node only has to move minimal data, without needing virtual nodes. With naive hash % num_shards, increasing from 4 to 5 shards moves ~80% of keys. With consistent hashing, only ~20% of keys move (the share belonging to the new shard).

Resharding is currently an offline operation via the built-in CLI:

  1. Stop the server.
  2. Run blobasaur shard migrate 4 5 --verify.
  3. Update num_shards in config.toml and start the server.

The migration tool moves keys whose target shard changed. With --verify, it checks that keys are in the expected shards and reports post-migration row counts.

Moving off SSDB

We rolled out Blobasaur in a phased deployment strategy:

  1. New workloads first: When we launched Kite Terminal mode, we pointed its workspace storage directly at Blobasaur.
  2. Dual-write and backfill: For existing workloads like chart preferences, we updated the services to dual-write to both SSDB and Blobasaur while running a background migration for historical keys. Reads went to Blobasaur first and fell back to SSDB on a cache miss or error.
  3. Cutover: On the client side, the only code change was switching from a single-node Redis client to a Redis Cluster client with the three Blobasaur node IPs.

After running dual-writes for a month with zero discrepancies, we turned off SSDB.

What we learned along the way

Deleting rows doesn’t shrink SQLite files

Early on, we noticed disk usage only grew, even after millions of keys expired or were deleted. By default, SQLite keeps freed pages on an internal freelist for future writes rather than returning space to the OS.

To fix this, we enabled PRAGMA auto_vacuum = INCREMENTAL across every shard and added a blobasaur shard vacuum subcommand to reclaim unused freelist pages within a set allocation (128 MB default). Since shrinking the actual database file in WAL mode requires a checkpoint, Blobasaur runs PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) right after executing an incremental vacuum.

Async writes have to be visible to every read

When async_write is enabled, a write returns OK while still sitting in the shard’s memory queue waiting for the next batch commit. To preserve read-your-writes consistency, queued writes are also placed in an in-memory pending map that reads check before querying SQLite.

During testing, we hit edge cases where certain read and existence-check paths bypassed this pending map or didn’t account for deletes. For example, a DEL followed immediately by a GET could return the old value from SQLite because the queued DEL hadn’t committed yet. We fixed this by storing explicit tombstones in the pending map and routing every read (GET, HGET, EXISTS, TTL) through it first.

In production, our p99 write latency normally sat below 5 ms, but we occasionally saw spikes to 30 to 50 ms.

We traced the spikes to the background TTL cleanup task. Initially, the cleanup worker opened its own write connection and ran a single large DELETE statement for all expired rows. That large DELETE contended with the shard’s main writer for SQLite’s single write lock, stalling normal client batches.

We fixed this in two ways: routing cleanup batches through the shard’s existing writer connection so they take turns cleanly with client writes, and bounding each pass with cleanup_chunk_size (1,000 rows by default). Since expired rows are already filtered out at read time, spreading physical deletion across smaller chunks eliminated the latency spikes without affecting correctness.

In production

Our current Blobasaur deployment runs as a three-node (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) cluster. Over a full trading session (09:00 to 15:30), p99 latency across all commands stays around 2 ms on every node, and p50 sits between 250 and 550 µs.

Broken down by command, HSET p99 sits around 2 ms, HGET p99 around 1.4 ms, and HDEL p99 mostly under 1 ms.

Blobasaur is open source under the AGPLv3 license and available on GitHub @iamd3vil/blobasaur. Find other projects from the Zerodha.tech hacker collective at 4th Cross Labs.

item.title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP (330 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://kapteko.com/15-million-webservers/, See on Hacker News

Nov 18, 2026

Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.

Web server

Instead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.

  1. listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket
  2. accept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket
  3. recv - receives data from a socket
  4. send - sends data
  5. close - closes

What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.

int main(void)
{
    // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port
    int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); 
    if (listen(server, 128) < 0)
        return 1;
    const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK";
    for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }
}

It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:

$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done
...
...
28232
program exited with error 1

Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.

$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768    60999

Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.

  • Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).
  • Ports 1-1024 require root.
  • Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.
  • Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.

Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Let’s simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server.

The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldn’t be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, we’ll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!

UPD. I’ve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didn’t get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Can’t we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?

Let’s use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. We’ll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:

// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it
int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]);
const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001;  // ex. 10.64.0.1
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i);  // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2

And now we can finally finish the article.

$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done
...
...
Out of memory

Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would take… 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.

Runtime

By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.

TLDR: We’re using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory isolation and replaces all syscalls with calls to our host handler, which lets us implement I/O however we like. To schedule multiple guests, we load them all into our main process’s memory and make the CPU constantly switch between guests - we become our own micro OS.

Since we need to save every byte and CPU cycle we can, we’re doomed to build another specialised runtime. Let’s get started. How much is 10GB divided by 15M, exactly?

Ten Great Britains divided by 15 million gives around half of kilo britain. Not much. If we run all our guests in our runtime, our custom scheduler needs to switch between them. What’s the absolute minimum state we need to preserve for each guest? We can ignore server initialisation and assume switches only happen within the main loop. Let’s take another look at the loop.

for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }

This code has only two state variables, server and client. Both are simple file descriptors. If our scheduler had to suspend a guest at any syscall point in this loop, we’d need to save the following state:

struct Context {
    pc: u64,        // Instruction address to return to
    fd_server: i32, // server file descriptor
    fd_client: i32, // client file descriptor
}

We only need 16 bytes per guest, so to run 15M guests in our runtime and be able to suspend them and switch between them, we would need 220MB of RAM. We’re playing it safe here - we don’t need the full u64 or i32, and with bit packing, we could probably get down to 8 bytes per guest. What else do we need?

$ codex "How much TCP connection takes?"
Idle connection takes zero, while active connection consumes around 5kb

Here’s what we get if we assume that only 1M of connections are active at any given moment.

  • 14M idle connections - 0 bytes
  • Scheduling state for 15M guests - 220MB
  • 1M active connections at 5kb each = 5GB

Only half of our RAM budget, yay! I don’t often exceed my own expectations. Let’s validate it:

int main(void) {
    // Run 14M of idle connections - just listen and do nothing
    // SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY!
    for (int i = 0; i < 14_000_000; i++) {
        int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); 
        listen(server, 1)
    }
}
$ ./run_15m_idle_servers
Out Of Memory
$ dmesg | tail -n 1
'SHOULD CONSUMER ZERO MEMORY' - what are you, stupid?

Looks like the kernel still has some leftover comments from Linus. I’m not stupid, but I have to admit I was below average here. While an LLM is a significant boost for learning, it’s too easy to accept its answers without thinking critically and feel ashamed later on. But hey, embarrassment is a cost of entry - let’s dive into networking in the kernel.

Networking in the kernel

Remember when I said that our simple server uses only 5 syscalls? I missed one that was right in front of me. Let me highlight it:

int main(void)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; ++i) {
        socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    }
}

That code will OOM in a 10GB VM. The socket syscall allocates around 3300 bytes, whether the socket is active, listening, or doing nothing. Linux was clearly written at a time when RAM was big and cheap, sigh. Let’s ask AI where all the memory goes:

StructsizeofDescription
struct tcp_sock2240BTCP state, queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, retransmit and delivery bookkeeping
struct socket_alloc768BA 128-byte struct socket with an embedded wait queue, plus a 608-byte sockfs inode and padding
struct file184BOpen-file operations, flags, credentials, reference count, and the pointer back to the socket
struct dentry192BThe sockfs pseudo-name, inode pointer, and VFS lookup and lifetime bookkeeping
Total3384B

Potato-potato, TLDR, the kernel uses that memory for many things. I was hoping to see some buffer: [u8; 3300], but it doesn’t look like we can optimise much without rewriting half the kernel. It’s Sunday and I have few tokens left, so we’ll have to think instead - how can we bypass the kernel?

What are our options? Engineering wisdom tells us that if we can’t solve a task, we’re working at the wrong level of abstraction. Hm… level, level, layer. Wait a minute! We started with HTTP and went level down to TCP/IP. That reminds me of something! Mom! Mom! Where are all my university books? I NEED THEM NOW!

The OSI model is… um… something I studied at university. Yeah, that’s a good definition. We started with our app and HTTP at the application layer, then went down to TCP/IP at the transport layer. There are three more layers below that. Can we go lower to get full control and solve our RAM problem? Oh yes, that’s exactly what operating at the network and data link layers lets us do. What about going to the lowest?

Clear.

Each layer wraps the data from the layer above it.

TCP/IP is stateful, but everything below is stateless. None of the lower layers know or care about the payload, so nothing prevents us from sending new IP packets or even Ethernet frames with our own handcrafted binary data. We just need to reimplement the TCP and IP stack ourselves. Are there any examples? Embedded folks have solved this millions of times. The most extreme case is Adam Dunkels’s Miniweb - it combines a custom TCP/IP implementation and an HTTP server that together need only 28 bytes (B-Y-T-E-S) to work.

There are plenty of less extreme, more mature implementations, though:

  • gVisor essentially reimplements the whole OS, including the network stack
  • Seastar is a whole runtime with its own network stack from the amazing team behind ScyllaDB
  • lwIP is a popular C implementation of TCP/IP
  • F-Stack uses FreeBSD’s TCP/IP stack

Go, C++, and C are nice languages (well, kinda), but they’re nowhere near as nice as our beloved Rust. So we’ll take smoltcp, which is purely amazing:

>smoltcp is a standalone, event-driven TCP/IP stack that is designed for
>bare-metal, real-time systems. smoltcp does not need heap allocation at all

So, cargo add smoltcp and call it a day? Not so fast. smoltcp is essentially a smart parser and can’t do I/O. How does it communicate with your network card? There are 3 ways:

  • TUN is a virtual network interface that the kernel provides. It operates at the IP layer
  • TAP is another kernel feature that operates one layer down, at the Ethernet layer
  • DPDK lets you communicate directly with the network card using Ethernet frames, completely bypassing the kernel

smoltcp is kind enough to provide the first two options out of the box, and they’re easy to use.

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let (mut device, config) = match std::env::args().nth(1).as_deref() {
        Some("tun") => (
            TunTapInterface::new("smoltun", Medium::Ip)?,
            Config::new(HardwareAddress::Ip),
        ),
        Some("tap") => (
            TunTapInterface::new("smoltap", Medium::Ethernet)?,
            Config::new(EthernetAddress([0x02, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2]).into()),
        ),
        _ => panic!("pass tun or tap"),
    };
    let mut iface = Interface::new(config, &mut device, Instant::now());
    iface.update_ip_addrs(|addrs| {
        addrs.push(IpCidr::new(IpAddress::v4(192, 0, 2, 2), 24)).unwrap();
    });
    let mut sockets = SocketSet::new(Vec::new());
    
    // Main network loop
    loop {
        let now = Instant::now();
        iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets);
        wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?;
    }
}

But what about the third option, DPDK? When you care about latency A LOT, every syscall is a bloody wound. The syscall itself might take 500ns, and copying data from the kernel to userspace might take another 1000ns, depending on the buffer size. That sounds tiny, but for perspective: it’s common for high-frequency trading firms to saturate 400Gbs network interfaces. That means processing up to 600 million packets per second, or roughly 1.7ns per packet.

DPDK lets your program communicate directly with the hardware network card using Ethernet frames, bypassing the entire kernel network stack. You read from and write to a memory-mapped buffer without syscalls: when you want to send data - you simply write it to the buffer and you’re done; when you want to read what you’ve received - it’s already there.

There’s another, less obvious advantage - what happens when a new packet arrives at your network device? An interrupt fires, the CPU core stops executing your app, switches to the kernel, processes the interrupt, and then goes back to your app. Now imagine A LOT of incoming packets, so many that your app gets interrupted all the time. It has a beautiful name, livelock, and I guess debugging it in production is its own level of hell. DPDK lets you avoid all that, but there’s a cost.

DPDK works by running a busy loop that takes up an entire CPU core. It constantly moves data between memory and the network device in both directions, kinda like that:

loop {
    send_from_app_memory_to_network();
    receive_from_network_to_app_memory();
}

There’s another, less obvious nuance. DPDK requires exclusive access to the network device because it uses a driver that operates at the hardware level - two drivers can’t work with the same device at the same time. Once you enable the DPDK driver for your network interface… it disappears from the OS. Yep, nothing in ifconfig, if you enable it over SSH, you’ll lose SSH access too. I can imagine a lot of funny stories coming out of that.

Actually, there’s a fourth option now - Linux now has an AF_XDP subsystem that does something similar. It lets you bypass the kernel network stack and uses the same idea of memory-mapped buffers to get zero-copy I/O in your app. The kernel still owns the device and interrupts still happen as usual. When a new packet arrives, the kernel runs a simple eBPF filter that decides whether to send it directly to the userspace buffer, bypassing the network stack, or process it normally. That means SSH still works. AF_XDP supports an alternative mode, SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL, which is even closer to DPDK: you get a busy loop with no interrupts at the cost of a CPU core. DPDK still beats it because it bypasses the kernel completely, but AF_XDP is very close (and simply easier to manage).

To support DPDK and AF_XDP in smoltcp, we only need to implement the Device trait with 3 methods if we want full control. Alternatively, we can use the existing crates rust-dpdk-net for DPDK and xsk-rs for AF_XDP to help us.

Now the final flow is:

  1. The runtime loads 15M web server guests into its memory
  2. The runtime scheduler starts executing guests one by one
  3. Guest syscalls are intercepted by the runtime and replaced by the smoltcp network stack and its adapters
  4. All 15M guests start listening, each on its own address
  5. The scheduler polls for incoming data from smoltcp adapters, wakes up a guest, makes it process the data, and switches to the next

And now we can finally finish the article. The kernel network stack uses up all the RAM at around 2.5M web servers, and RPS drops as we run more servers. With smoltcp, RAM usage grows slower - 620 bytes per idle server and around a kilobyte for an active one, we got to 16M of servers. DPDK is clearly the beast in this benchmark, with AF_XDP just behind it:

Why is this so exciting? It means that by moving the network stack to userland, you can get full control on RAM usage and improve performance. And with custom runtime, you can simply run guests faster.

Simply is a bit of a stretch - building a proof of concept is easy. Building a compatible Linux runtime and reimplementing all the syscalls with 100% POSIX compatibility take a bit more thought. And another article.

References

  • https://github.com/artemyarulin/AI10M/tree/main/poc/ten-million-webservers source
  • https://medium.com/beyond-localhost/how-we-handle-15M-websocket-connections-on-a-single-server-8917c3952f59 great overview of DPDK
  • https://doc.dpdk.org/guides/index.html DPDK main documentation site
  • https://docs.kernel.org/networking/af_xdp.html AF_XDP overview

Your deployment

The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.

Framework Status on an affected Ruby
Rails Affected
Sinatra (classic style) Affected
Other frameworks and plain Rack Not exposed by default

Self-hosted software

The latest version of the following popular software bundles an affected Ruby.

Software Bundled Ruby Status
GitLab 19.6.0 3.3.13 Affected
GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 4.0.9 Affected
Mastodon 4.7.5 4.0.9 Affected
OpenProject 17.9.7 4.0.9 Affected
Discourse 2026.10.1 3.4.7 Affected
Chatwoot 4.20.0 3.4.4 Affected

Updated 19 November 2026 at 10:00 UTC.

Your deployment

Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

Self-hosted software

Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.

Technical details

Root cause

Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital ß. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).

The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each ß adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.

Primitive

A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.

Proof of concept

We'll be publishing a proof of concept in a week, once people have had time to upgrade.

item.title: AI will not make you rich (2025) (105 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://colossus.com/article/ai-will-not-make-you-rich/, See on Hacker News

Click here to subscribe to print for your office or home.

Fortunes are made by entrepreneurs and investors when revolutionary technologies enable waves of innovative, investable companies. Think of the railroad, the Bessemer process, electric power, the internal combustion engine, or the microprocessor—each of which, like a stray spark in a fireworks factory, set off decades of follow-on innovations, permeated every part of society, and catapulted a new set of inventors and investors into power, influence, and wealth.

Yet some technological innovations, though societally transformative, generate little in the way of new wealth; instead, they reinforce the status quo. Fifteen years before the microprocessor, another revolutionary idea, shipping containerization, arrived at a less propitious time, when technological advancement was a Red Queen’s race, and inventors and investors were left no better off for non-stop running.

Anyone who invests in the new new thing must answer two questions: First, how much value will this innovation create? And second, who will capture it? Information and communication technology (ICT) was a revolution whose value was captured by startups and led to thousands of newly rich founders, employees, and investors. In contrast, shipping containerization was a revolution whose value was spread so thin that in the end, it made only a single founder temporarily rich and only a single investor a little bit richer.

Is generative AI more like the former or the latter? Will it be the basis of many future industrial fortunes, or a net loser for the investment community as a whole, with a few zero-sum winners here and there?

There are ways to make money investing in the fruits of AI, but they will depend on assuming the latter—that it is once again a less propitious time for inventors and investors, that AI model builders and application companies will eventually compete each other into an oligopoly, and that the gains from AI will accrue not to its builders but to customers. A lot of the money pouring into AI is therefore being invested in the wrong places, and aside from a couple of lucky early investors, those who make money will be the ones with the foresight to get out early.

The microprocessor was revolutionary, but the people who invented it at Intel in 1971 did not see it that way—they just wanted to avoid designing desktop calculator chipsets from scratch every time. But outsiders realized they could use the microprocessor to build their own personal computers, and enthusiasts did. Thousands of tinkerers found configurations and uses that Intel never dreamed of. This distributed and permissionless invention kicked off a “great surge of development,” as the economist Carlota Perez calls it, triggered by technology but driven by economic and societal forces.[1]

There was no real demand for personal computers in the early 1970s; they were expensive toys. But the experimenters laid the technical groundwork and built a community. Then, around 1975, a step-change in the cost of microprocessors made the personal computer market viable. The Intel 8080 had an initial list price of $360 ($2,300 in today’s dollars). MITS could barely turn a profit on its Altair at a bulk price of $75 each ($490 today). But when MOS Technologies started selling its 6502 for $25 ($150 today), Steve Wozniak could afford to build a prototype Apple. The 6502 and the similarly priced Zilog Z80 forced Intel’s prices down. The nascent PC community started spawning entrepreneurs and a score of companies appeared, each with a slightly different product.

You couldn’t have known in the mid-1970s that the PC (and PC-like products, such as ATMs, POS terminals, smartphones, etc.) would revolutionize everything. While Steve Jobs was telling investors that every household would someday have a personal computer (a wild underestimate, as it turned out), others questioned the need for personal computers at all. As late as 1979, Apple’s ads didn’t tell you what a personal computer could do—it asked what you did with it.[2] The established computer manufacturers (IBM, HP, DEC) had no interest in a product their customers weren’t asking for. Nobody “needed” a computer, and so PCs weren’t bought—they were sold. Flashy startups like Apple and Sinclair used hype to get noticed, while companies with footholds in consumer electronics like Atari, Commodore, and Tandy/RadioShack used strong retail connections to put their PCs in front of potential customers. 

The market grew slowly at first, accelerating only as experiments led to practical applications like the spreadsheet, introduced in 1979. As use grew, observation of use caused a reduction in uncertainty, leading to more adoption in a self-reinforcing cycle. This kind of gathering momentum takes time in every technological wave: It took almost 30 years for electricity to reach half of American households, for example, and it took about the same amount of time for personal computers.[3] When a technological revolution changes everything, it takes a huge amount of innovation, investment, storytelling, time, and plain old work. It also sucks up all the money and talent available. Like Kuhn’s paradigms in science, any technology not part of the wave’s techno-economic paradigm will seem like a sideshow.[4]

The nascent growth of PCs attracted investors—venture capitalists—who started making risky bets on new companies. This development incentivized more inventors, entrepreneurs, and researchers, which in turn drew in more speculative capital.

Companies like IBM, the computing behemoth before the PC, saw poor relative performance. They didn’t believe the PC could survive long enough to become capable in their market and didn’t care about new, small markets that wanted a cheaper solution.

Retroactively, we give the PC pioneers the powers of prophets rather than visionaries. But at the time, nobody outside of a small group of early adopters paid any attention. Establishment media like The New York Times didn’t take the PC seriously until after IBM’s was introduced in August 1981. In the entire year of 1976, when Apple Computer was founded, the NYT mentioned PCs only four times.[5] Apparently, only the crazy ones, the misfits, the rebels, and the troublemakers were paying attention.

It’s the element of surprise that should strike us most forcefully when we compare the early days of the computer revolution to today. No one took note of personal computers in the 1970s. In 2025, AI is all we seem to talk about.

Big companies hate surprises. That’s why uncertainty makes a perfect moat for startups. Apple would never have survived IBM entering the market in 1979, and only lived to compete another day after raising $100 million in its 1980 IPO. It was the only remaining competitor after the IBM-induced winnowing.[6]

As the tech took hold and started to show promise, innovations in software, memory, and peripherals like floppy disk drives and modems joined it. They reinforced one another, with each advance putting pressure on the technologies adjacent to it. When any part of the system held back the other parts, investors rushed to fund that sector. As increases in PC memory allowed more complicated software, for example, there became a need for more external storage, which caused VC Dave Marquardt to invest in disk drive manufacturer Seagate in 1980. Seagate gave Marquardt a 40x return when it went public in 1981. Other investors noticed, and some $270 million was plowed into the industry in the following three years.[7]

Money also poured into the underlying infrastructure—fiber optic networks, chip making, etc.—so that capacity was never a bottleneck. Companies which used the new technological system to outperform incumbents began to take market share, and even staid competitors realized they needed to adopt the new thing or die. The hype became a froth which became an investment bubble: the dot-com frenzy of the late 1990s. The ICT wave was therefore similar to previous ones—like the investment mania of the 1830s and the Roaring ‘20s, which followed the infrastructure buildout of canals and railways, respectively—in which the human response to each stage predictably generated the next.

When the dot-com bubble popped, society found it disapproved of the excesses in the sector and governments found they had the popular support to reassert authority over the tech companies and their investors. This put a brake on the madness. Instead of the reckless innovation of the bubble, companies started to expand into proven markets, and financiers moved from speculating to investing. Entrepreneurs began to focus on finding applications rather than on innovating the underlying technologies. Technological improvements continued, but change became more evolutionary than revolutionary.

As change slowed, companies gained the confidence to invest for the longer term. They began to combine various parts of the system in new ways to create value for a wider group of users. The massive overbuilding of fiber optic telecom networks and other infrastructure during the frenzy left plenty of cheap capacity, keeping the costs of expansion down. It was a great time to be a businessperson and investor.

In contrast, society did not need a bubble to pop to start excoriating AI. Given that the backlash to tech has been going on for a decade, this seems normal to us. But the AI backlash differs from the general high regard, earlier in the cycle, enjoyed by the likes of Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos, and others who built big tech businesses. The world hates change, and only gave tech a pass in the ‘80s and ‘90s because it all still seemed reversible: it could be made to go away if it turned out badly. This gave the early computer innovators some leeway to experiment. Now that everyone knows computers are here to stay, AI is not allowed the same wait-and-see attitude. It is seen as part of the ICT revolution.

Perez, the economist, breaks each technological wave into four predictable phases: irruption, frenzy, synergy, and maturity. Each has a characteristic investment profile.

The middle two, frenzy and synergy, are the easy ones for investors. Frenzy is when everyone piles in and investors are rewarded for taking big risks on unproven ideas, culminating in the bubble, when paper profits disappear. When rationality returns, the synergy phase begins, as companies make their products usable and productive for a wide array of users. Synergy pays those who are patient, picky, and can bring more than just money to the table.

Irruption and maturity are more difficult to invest in.

Investing in the 1970s was harder than it might look in hindsight. To invest from 1971 through 1975, you had to be either a true believer or a conglomerator with a knuckle-headed diversification strategy. Intel was a great investment, though it looked at first like a previous-wave electronics company. MOS Technologies was founded in 1969 to compete with Texas Instruments but sold a majority of itself to Allen-Bradley to stay afloat. Zilog was funded in 1975 by Exxon (Exxon!). Apple was a great investment, but it had none of the hallmarks of what VCs look for, as the PC was still a solution in search of a problem.

It was later irruption, in the early 1980s, when great opportunities proliferated: PC makers (Compaq, Dell), software and operating systems (Microsoft, Electronic Arts, Adobe), peripherals (Seagate), workstations (Sun), and computer stores (Businessland), among others. If you invested in the winners, you did well. But there was still more money than ideas, which meant that it was no golden age for investing. By 1983, there were more than 70 companies competing in the disk drive sector alone, and valuations collapsed. There were plenty of people whose fortunes were established in the 1970s and 1980s, and many VCs made their names in that era. But the biggest advantage to being an irruption-stage investor was building institutional knowledge to invest early and well in the frenzy and synergy phases.

Investing in the maturity phase is even more difficult. In irruption, it’s hard to see what will happen; in maturity, nothing much happens at all. The uncertainty about what will work and how customers and society will react is almost gone. Things are predictable, and everyone acts predictably.

The lack of dynamism allows the successful synergy companies to remain entrenched (see: the Nifty 50 and FAANG), but growth becomes harder. They start to enter each other’s markets, conglomerate, raise prices, and cut costs. The era of products priced to entice new customers ends, and quality suffers. The big companies continue to embrace the idea of revolutionary innovation, but feel the need to control how their advances are used. R&D spending is redirected from product and process innovation toward increasingly fruitless attempts to find ways to extend the current paradigm. Companies frame this as a drive to win, but it’s really a fear of losing.

Innovation can happen during maturity, sometimes spectacularly. But because these innovations only find support if they fit into the current wave’s paradigm, they are easily captured in the dominant companies’ gravity wells. This means making money as an entrepreneur or investor in them is almost impossible. Generative AI is clearly being captured by the dominant ICT companies, which raises the question of whether this time will be different for inventors and investors—a different question from whether AI itself is a revolutionary technology.

Shipping containerization was a late-wave innovation that changed the world, kicked off our modern era of globalization, resulted in profound changes to society and the economy, and contributed to rapid growth in well-being. But there were, perhaps, only one or two people who made real money investing in it.

The year 1956 was late in the previous wave. But that year, the company soon to be known as SeaLand revolutionized freight shipping with the launch of the first containership, the Ideal-X. SeaLand’s founder, Malcom McLean, had an epiphany that the job to be done by truckers, railroads, and shipping lines was to move goods from shipper to destination, not to drive trucks, fill boxcars, or lade boats. SeaLand allowed freight to transfer seamlessly from one mode to another, saving time, making shipping more predictable, and cutting costs—both the costs of loading, unloading, and reloading, and the cost of a ship sitting idly in port as it was loaded and unloaded.[8]

The benefits of containerization, if it could be made to happen, were obvious. Everybody could see the efficiencies, and customers don’t care how something gets to where they can buy it, as long as it does. But longshoremen would lose work, politicians would lose the votes of those who lost work, port authorities would lose the support of the politicians, federal regulators would be blamed for adverse consequences, railroads might lose freight to shipping lines, shipping lines might lose freight to new shipping lines, and it would all cost a mint. Most thought McLean would never be able to make it work.

McLean squeezed through the cracks of the opposition he faced. He bought and retrofitted war surplus ships, lowering costs. He went after the coastal shipping trade, a dying business in the age of the new interstates, to avoid competition. He set up shop in Newark, NJ, rather than the shipping hub of Hell’s Kitchen, to get buy-in from the port authority and avoid Manhattan congestion. And he made a deal with the New York longshoremen’s union, which was only possible because he was a small player whom they figured was not a threat.

But competitors and regulators moved too quickly for McLean to seize the few barriers to entry that might have been available to him: domination of the ports, exclusive agreements with shippers or other forms of transportation, standardization on proprietary technology, etc.[9] When it started to look like it might work, around 1965, the obvious advantages of containerization meant that every large shipping line entered the business, and competition took off. Even though containerized freight was less than 1% of total trade by 1968, the number of containerships was already ramping fast.[10] Capacity outstripped demand for years. 

The increase in competition led to a rate war, which led to squeezed profits, which in turn led to consolidation and cartels. Meanwhile, the cost of building ever-larger container ships and the port facilities to deal with them meant the business became hugely capital intensive. McLean saw the writing on the wall and sold SeaLand to R.J. Reynolds in January 1969. He was, perhaps, the only entrepreneur to get out unscathed.

It took a long time for the end-to-end vision to be realized. But around 1980, a dramatic drop began in the cost of sea freight.[11] This contributed to a boom in international trade,[12] and allowed manufacturers to move away from higher-wage to lower-wage countries, making containerization irreversible.

Some people did make money, of course; someone always does. McLean did, as did shipping magnate Daniel Ludwig, who had invested $8.5 million in SeaLand’s predecessor, McLean Industries, at $8.50 per share in 1965 and sold in 1969 for $50 per share.[13] Shipbuilders made money, too: between 1967 and 1972, some $10 billion ($80 billion in 2025 dollars) was spent building containerships. The contractors that built the new container ports also made money. And, later, shipping lines that consolidated and dominated the business, like Maersk and Evergreen, became very large. But, “for R.J. Reynolds, and for other companies that had chased fast growth by buying into container shipping in the late 1960s, their investments brought little but disappointment.”[14] Aside from McLean and Ludwig, it is hard to find anyone who became rich from containerization itself, because competition and capex costs made it hard to grow fast or achieve high margins.

The business ended up being dominated primarily by the previous incumbents, and the margins went to the companies shipping goods, not the ones they shipped through. Companies like IKEA benefited from cheap shipping, going from a provincial Scandinavian company in 1972 to the world’s largest furniture retailer by 2008; container shipping was a perfect fit for IKEA’s flat-pack furniture. Others, like Walmart, used the predictability enabled by containerization to lower inventory and its associated costs.

With hindsight, it’s easy to see how you could have invested in containerization: not in the container shipping industry itself, but in the industries that benefited from containerization. But even here, the success of companies like Walmart, Costco, and Target was coupled with the failure of others. The fallout from containerization set Sears and Woolworth on downward spirals, put the final nail in the coffin of Montgomery Ward and A&P, and drove Macy’s into bankruptcy before it was rescued and downsized by Federated. Meanwhile, in North Carolina, “the furniture capital of the world,” furniture makers tried to compete with IKEA by importing cheap pieces from China. They ended up being replaced by their suppliers.[15]

If there had been more time to build moats, there might have been a few dominant containerization companies, and the people behind them would be at the top of the Forbes 400, while their investors would be legendary. But moats take time to build and, unlike the personal computer, the adoption of containerization wasn’t a surprise—every business with interests at stake had a strategic plan immediately.

The economist Joseph Schumpeter said “perfect competition is and always has been temporarily suspended whenever anything new is being introduced.”[16] But containerization shows this isn’t true at the end of tech waves. And because there is no economic profit during perfect competition, there is no money to be made by innovators during maturity. Like containerization, the introduction of AI did not lead to a period of protected profits for its innovators. It led to an immediate competitive free-for-all.

Let’s grant that generative AI is revolutionary (but also that, as is becoming increasingly clear, this particular tech is now already in an evolutionary stage). It will create a lot of value for the economy, and investors hope to capture some of it. When, who, and how depends on whether AI is the end of the ICT wave, or the beginning of a new one. 

If AI had started a new wave, there would have been an extended period of uncertainty and experimentation. There would have been a population of early adopters experimenting with their own models. When thousands or millions of tinkerers use the tech to solve problems in entirely new ways, its uses proliferate. But because they are using models owned by the big AI companies, their ability to fully experiment is limited to what’s allowed by the incumbents, who have no desire to permit an extended challenge to the status quo.

This doesn’t mean AI can’t start the next technological revolution. It might, if experimentation becomes cheap, distributed and permissionless—like Wozniak cobbling together computers in his garage, Ford building his first internal combustion engine in his kitchen, or Trevithick building his high-pressure steam engine as soon as James Watt’s patents expired. When any would-be innovator can build and train an LLM on their laptop and put it to use in any way their imagination dictates, it might be the seed of the next big set of changes—something revolutionary rather than evolutionary. But until and unless that happens, there can be no irruption.

AI is instead the epitome of the ICT wave. The computing visionaries of the 1960s set out to build a machine that could think, which their successors eventually did, by extending gains in algorithms, chips, data, and data center infrastructure. Like containerization, AI is an extension of something that came before, and therefore no one is surprised by what it can and will do. In the 1970s, it took time for people to wrap their heads around the desirability of powerful and ubiquitous computing. But in 2025, machines that think better than previous machines are easy for people to understand.

Consider the extent to which the progress of AI rhymes with the business evolution of containerization:

In the “AI rhymes” column, the first four items are already underway. How you should invest depends on whether you believe Nos. 5–7 are next.

Economists are predicting that AI will increase global GDP somewhere between 1%[17] to more than 7%[18] over the next decade, which is $1–7 trillion of new value created. The big question is where that money will stick as it flows through the value chain.

Most AI market overviews have a score or more categories, breaking each of them into customer and industry served. But these will change dramatically over the next few years. You could, instead, just follow the money to simplify the taxonomy of companies:

What the history of containerization suggests is that, if you aren’t already an investor in a model company, you shouldn’t bother. Sam Altman and a few other early movers may make a fortune, as McLean and Ludwig did. But the huge costs of building and running a model, coupled with intense competition, means there will, in the end, be only a few companies, each funded and owned by the largest tech companies. If you’re already an investor, congratulations: There will be consolidation, so you might get an exit.

Domain-specific models—like Cursor or Harvey—will be part of the consolidation. These are probably the most valuable models. But fine-tuning is relatively cheap, and there are big economies of scope. On the other hand, just as Google had to buy Invite Media in 2010 to figure out how to sell to ad agencies, domain-specific model companies that have earned the trust of their customers will be prime acquisition targets. And although it seems possible that models which generate things other than language—like Midjourney or Runway—might use their somewhat different architecture to carve out a separate technological path, the LLM companies have easily entered this space as well. Whether this applies to companies like Osmo remains to be seen.

While it’s too late to invest in the model companies, the profusion of those using the models to solve specific problems is ongoing: Perplexity, InflectionAI, Writer, Abridge, and a hundred others. But if any of these become very valuable, the model companies will take their earnings, either through discriminatory pricing or vertical integration. Success, in other words, will mean defeat—always a bad thesis. At some point, model companies and app companies will converge: There will simply be AI companies, and only a few of them. There will be some winners, as always, but investments in the app layer as a whole will lose money. 

The same caveat applies, however: If an app company can build a customer base or an amazing team, it might be acquired. But these companies aren’t really technology companies at all; they are building a market on spec and have to be priced as such. A further caveat is that there will be investors who make a killing arbitraging FOMO-panicked acquirors willing to massively overpay. But this is not really “investing.”

There might be an investment opportunity in companies that manage the interface between the AI giants and their customers, or protect company data from the model companies—like Hugging Face or Glean—because these businesses are by nature independent of the models. But no analogue in the post-containerization shipping market became very large. Even the successful intermediation companies in the AI space will likely end up mid-sized because the model companies will not allow them to gain strategic leverage—another consequence of the absence of surprise.

When an industry is going to be big but there is uncertainty about how it will play out, it often makes sense to swim upstream to the industry’s suppliers. In the case of AI, this means the chip providers, data companies, and cloud/data center companies: SambaNova, Scale AI, and Lambda, as well as those that have been around for a long time, like Nvidia and Bloomberg.

The case for data is mixed. General data—i.e., things most people know, including everything anyone knew more than, say, 10 years ago, and most of what was learned after that—is a commodity. There may be room for a few companies to do the grunt work of collating and tagging it, but since the collating and tagging might best be done by AI itself, there will not be a lot of pricing leverage. Domain-specific models will need specialist data, and other models will try to answer questions about the current moment. Specific, timely, and hard to reproduce data will be valuable. This is not a new market, of course—Bloomberg and others have done well by it. A more concentrated customer base will lower prices for this data, while wider use will raise revenues. On balance, this will probably be a plus for the industry, though not a huge one. There will be new companies built, but only a couple worth investing in.

The high capex of AI companies will primarily be spent with the infrastructure companies. These companies are already valued with this expectation, so there won’t be an upside surprise. But consider that shipbuilding benefited from containerization from 1965 until demand collapsed after about 1973.[19] If AI companies consolidate or otherwise act in concert, even a slight downturn that forces them to conserve cash could turn into a serious, sudden, and long-lasting decline in infrastructure spending. This would leave companies like Nvidia and its emerging competitors—who must all make long-term commitments to suppliers and for capacity expansion—unable to lower costs to match the new, smaller market size. Companies priced for an s-curve are overpriced if there’s a peak and decline.

All of which means that investors shouldn’t swim upstream, but fish downstream: companies whose products rely on achieving high-quality results from somewhat ambiguous information will see increased productivity and higher profits. These sectors include professional services, healthcare, education, financial services, and creative services, which together account for between a third and a half of global GDP and have not seen much increased productivity from automation. AI can help lower costs, but as with containerization, how individual businesses incorporate lower costs into their strategies—and what they decide to do with the savings—will determine success. To put it bluntly, using cost savings to increase profits rather than grow revenue is a loser’s game.

The companies that will benefit most rapidly are those whose strategies are already conditional on lowering costs. IKEA’s longtime strategy was to sell quality furniture for low prices and make it up on volume. After containerization made it possible for them to go worldwide, IKEA became the world’s largest retailer and Ingvar Kamprad (the IK of IKEA) became a billionaire. Similarly, Walmart, whose strategy was high volume and low prices in underserved markets, benefited from both cost savings and just-in-time supply chains, allowing increased product variety and lower inventory costs.

Today’s knowledge-work companies that already prioritize the same values are the least risky way to bet on AI, but new companies will form or re-form with a high-volume, low-cost strategy, just as Costco did in the early 1980s. New companies will compete with the incumbents, but with a clean slate and hindsight. Regardless, there are few barriers to entry, so each of these firms will face stiff competition and operate in fragmented markets. Experienced management and flawless execution will be key.

Being an entrepreneur will be a fabulous proposition in these sectors. Being an investor will be harder. Companies will not need much private capital—IKEA never needed to raise risk capital, and Costco raised only one round in 1983 before going public in 1985—because implementing cost-savings technology is not capital intensive. As with containerization, there will be a long lag between technology trigger and the best investments. The opportunities will be later.

Stock pickers will also make money, but they need to be choosy. At the high end of projections, an additional 7% in GDP growth over 10 years within one third of the economy gives a tailwind of only about 2% per year to these companies—even less if productivity growth from older ICT products abates. The primary value shift will be to companies that are embracing the strategic implications of AI from companies that are not, the way Walmart benefited from Sears, which took advantage of cheaper goods prices but did not reinvent itself.

Consumers, however, will be the biggest beneficiaries. Previous waves of mechanization benefited labor productivity in manufacturing, driving prices down and saving consumers money. But increased labor productivity in manufacturing also led to higher manufacturing wages. Wages in services businesses had to rise to compete, even though these businesses did not benefit from productivity gains. This caused the price of services to rise.[20] The share of household spending on food and clothing went from 55% in 1918 to 16% in 2023,[21] but the cost of knowledge-intensive services like healthcare and education have grown well above inflation. 

Something similar will happen with AI: Knowledge-intensive services will get cheaper, allowing consumers to buy more of them, while services that require person-to-person interaction will get more expensive, taking up a greater percentage of household spending. This points to obvious opportunities in both. But the big news is that most of the new value created by AI will be captured by consumers, who should see a wider variety of knowledge-intensive goods at reasonable prices, and wider and more affordable access to services like medical care, education, and advice.

There is nothing better than the beginning of a new wave, when the opportunities to envision, invent, and build world-changing companies leads to money, fame, and glory. But there is nothing more dangerous for investors and entrepreneurs than wishful thinking. The lessons learned from investing in tech over the last 50 years are not the right ones to apply now. The way to invest in AI is to think through the implications of knowledge workers becoming more efficient, to imagine what markets this efficiency unlocks, and to invest in those. For decades, the way to make money was to bet on what the new thing was. Now, you have to bet on the opportunities it opens up.

Jerry Neumann is a retired venture investor, writing and teaching about innovation.
